name: Sign in with Apple
plain: A login where Apple confirms identity and can hide the person's real email address.
meaning: Site gets a sub ID, email (real or relay) and email_verified; name only on first sign in. is_private_email and real_user_status (0 unsupported, 1 unknown, 2 likely real) are returned. Required in App Store apps that offer other social logins.

web.api: AppleID JS or redirect; OIDC id_token

access.persistence: Authorisation lasts until the person revokes it in Apple Account settings
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

limits.headline: Can sign you in with Apple and get a real or hidden email address
limits.user_action: You tap Sign in with Apple and confirm with Face ID, Touch ID or your Apple password
can: Receive a stable ID for you on that app or site
Get your real email or a private relay address you choose
Learn whether the email is verified and whether you look like a real person
Get your name, but only the first time you sign in
cannot: Get your real email if you pick Hide My Email
See your Apple purchases, photos or contacts
Get your name again on later sign ins
limits.differs: On iPhone the sign in is one tap with Face ID. On Android and other browsers it opens an Apple web page.

story.what_it_is: Sign in using your Apple account, with an option to hide your real email.

marketing.name: Sign in with Apple
marketing.pitch: Apple sells it as a fast, private way to sign in to apps and sites, with Face ID and the choice to hide your email.

marketing.name: Hide My Email
marketing.pitch: Apple describes a random email address that forwards to your inbox so you do not share your real one.

story.for_you: You tap a black Apple button and confirm with Face ID or Touch ID. You choose to share your real email or a random one that forwards to you. The site never gets your Apple password.
story.for_makers: Makers get quick sign ups with a confirmed identity and fewer fake accounts. They must offer it if they offer other social logins on iPhone apps, and they get a relay email they can still send to.

use_cases.example: A game's web page lets players create an account with Apple, so progress follows them from iPhone to browser.
A shopper signs up at a new store with a hidden email and later cuts off the store's marketing by turning off the relay.
A streaming or news site gets a verified account in two taps, with less password reset support.
Because the site only sees a relay address, email ad matching across sites gets harder, so marketers lean on first party data.
A site treats the Apple signal that this looks like a real person as extra proof against bot sign ups.
A work or notes web app lets Mac and iPhone users sign in without a new password.

risks: Apple sees where you sign in

technical_bounds: Name and email shared only on first authorisation
Relay address can be turned off by the person
Sender domains must be registered to reach the relay

abuse: Covert linking of accounts if users reuse the real email
